title: Training-Free Bayesian Filtering with Generative Emulators
claim: Skill degrades as ensemble size grows, and the proposed filter attains the lowest error and stays stable at small ensembles.
layout: 1 panel, line plot, log-log axes, legend top-right, markers per method
description: A single line chart with a logarithmic y-axis labeled Skill, from 10^0 to 10^1. The x-axis is Number of particles, from 2^1 to 2^10. Six smooth curves have distinct colors and marker shapes: Forecast in blue circles, BPF in orange squares, EnKF in green triangles, EnFF in red diamonds, EnSF in purple crosses, and FA-APF in brown plus signs. The legend sits at the top right. Forecast stays almost flat near 7. BPF drops steeply from about 9 to below 1. EnSF and EnFF fall gradually. EnKF collapses quickly and then plateaus near 0.7. FA-APF is lowest throughout, at about 0.9 down to 0.6. Light grid lines run behind the curves. The eye goes first to the steep drops and the low brown curve at the bottom.
caption: Evolution of the average skill as a function of the number of ensemble members.
abstract: Bayesian filtering is a well-known problem that aims to estimate plausible states of a dynamical system from observations. Among existing approaches to solve this problem, particle filters are theoretically exact for non-linear dynamics and observations, but suffer from poor scalability in high dimensions. In this work, we show that diffusion-based emulators of dynamical systems can be used to implement, without additional training, an optimal variant of particle filters that has remained largely unexplored due to implementation challenges with classical numerical solvers. Experiments on nonlinear chaotic systems, including atmospheric dynamics, demonstrate that the proposed approach successfully scales particle filtering to high-dimensional settings.
